name: Lunar Prospector
intro: Lunar Prospector orbited the Moon for a year and a half, mapping what its surface is made of and finding hints of ice at the poles. At the end it was crashed into a permanently shadowed crater near the south pole, now called Shoemaker. Its crater lies hidden in permanent darkness. The Sun never climbs above the big crater’s rim here, so the faint light is turned up for you. Look up: a see-through copy of Lunar Prospector hangs over the spot, just as it looked a moment before impact.
whyLeft: Its fuel was almost gone, so NASA used the last of it for one final experiment: crash into a dark crater and see if water vapour splashed up.
repurpose: The ice it hinted at is the prize: NASA’s plans for the south pole include turning ice like this into water, air and rocket fuel.
funFact: The whole mission cost $62.8 million, and the spacecraft had no computer on board: every command came from controllers on Earth.

hotspots.title: Hidden crash site
hotspots.text: Lunar Prospector hit the floor of Shoemaker crater, which never sees sunlight. Its crater is lost in the darkness, so the spot is shown only on maps.

photo.alt: A map-like view of the Moon’s cratered south pole with a black circle near the centre
photo.caption: The Moon’s south pole in a 1999 NASA visualization; the circle marks the area where Lunar Prospector crashed.

hotspots.title: No splash seen
hotspots.text: Telescopes on Earth and in space watched the crash, hoping to see water vapour. They saw no sign of it. A good experiment can still give a “no” answer.

hotspots.title: Hints of ice
hotspots.text: Lunar Prospector’s neutron detector found extra hydrogen near both poles, a strong hint that water ice is hiding in dark craters like this one.

source.label: NASA SVS: Lunar Prospector hydrogen at the south pole

photo.alt: A colour map of the Moon showing hydrogen, with blue near the poles
photo.caption: Lunar Prospector’s hydrogen map: blue shows more hydrogen, red shows less.

hotspots.title: Small but busy
hotspots.text: Lunar Prospector was a small drum with three long arms holding its instruments away from the body. It had no camera at all, just detectors that ‘smelled’ the Moon’s surface.

photo.alt: Lunar Prospector, a small drum-shaped spacecraft, on top of its rocket motor in a clean room
photo.caption: Lunar Prospector on Earth before launch, sitting on the rocket motor that pushed it to the Moon.

hotspots.title: A scientist’s resting place
hotspots.text: Lunar Prospector carried part of the ashes of Eugene Shoemaker, a geologist who helped train Apollo astronauts. The crater it hit now carries his name.

hotspots.title: Rock mapper
hotspots.text: This instrument measured gamma rays coming up from the ground below. From orbit, it mapped where the Moon’s main kinds of rock are.

hotspots.title: Magnet sensor
hotspots.text: The magnetometer rides at the very end, another 1.1 m beyond the boom’s tip, far from the spacecraft’s own electronics. It found that the Moon has only small, patchy magnetic fields.
